::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What this lesson is for

A table of numbers is hard to talk about in a meeting. A **picture** is not.

In this lesson you turn one of your own totals into a simple **bar chart**. It is the kind of picture you
can put in a report, or show to a supervisor. It takes one new command.

Press **Run** on each box. Remember: **you cannot break anything.**
:::

## First, one question from last time

Bring back one thing from the last lesson. A wrong answer costs nothing.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof recall_group = Inputs.radio(
  ["One row for each group", "One row altogether", "The same rows as before"],
  { label: "When you group_by() and then summarise(), what do you get back?" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`${
  // `== null` on purpose: Inputs.radio starts at null, not undefined, when nothing is picked.
  recall_group == null
    ? '<div class="alert alert-light py-2">Pick an answer above.</div>'
    : recall_group === "One row for each group"
      ? '<div class="alert alert-success py-2"><strong>Yes.</strong> One row of answer for each group. Two districts give two rows. That is exactly what a bar chart needs: <strong>one bar for each row</strong>.</div>'
      : '<div class="alert alert-warning py-2"><strong>Have another look.</strong> Grouping gives you <strong>one row for each group</strong>. Two districts give two rows, not one and not five. Hold on to that, because each of those rows becomes one bar.</div>'
}`
```

## Before we start

{{< include _before-we-start.qmd >}}

## A chart is just a table, drawn

The last lesson ended with a table of totals. A chart shows **the same numbers**, drawn as bars. Nothing
new is calculated. So a chart is always **two steps**.

**Step one: work out the totals**, exactly as you did last lesson, and give them a name. Here that name is
`totals`. Press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
totals <- example |>
  group_by(gaul_2_name) |>
  summarise(total_kg = sum(catch_kg))

totals
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** two rows. Shimoni **20** kg and Vanga **14** kg. Nothing has been drawn yet. You
have only given the answer a name, so you can use it again in the next box.
:::

**Step two: draw it.** Every box from here on uses the `totals` table you just made, so run the box above
first. If you ever see `object 'totals' not found`, that is all it means.

The command is **`barplot()`**, and it needs two things:

- the **heights** of the bars, `totals$total_kg`
- the **labels** under them, `totals$gaul_2_name`

Remember the `$` sign from the first lesson. It means "this column of that table".

**Before you run it, have a guess.**

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof predict_bar = Inputs.radio(
  ["3 kg — the smallest catch", "12 kg — the biggest single catch", "20 kg — the total for Shimoni"],
  { label: "How tall will the Shimoni bar be?" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`${
  // `== null` on purpose: Inputs.radio starts at null, not undefined, when nothing is picked.
  predict_bar == null
    ? '<div class="alert alert-light py-2">Pick an answer above, then press Run below to check it.</div>'
    : predict_bar === "20 kg — the total for Shimoni"
      ? '<div class="alert alert-success py-2"><strong>Yes — 20 kg.</strong> The chart draws the <code>totals</code> table, not the original rows. So each bar is that district\'s <strong>total</strong>.</div>'
      : '<div class="alert alert-warning py-2"><strong>Have another look.</strong> The chart draws the <code>totals</code> table from the box above, not the five original rows. Shimoni\'s row in <code>totals</code> says <strong>20</strong>, so that is the height of its bar.</div>'
}`
```

Now press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
barplot(totals$total_kg, names.arg = totals$gaul_2_name)
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** two grey bars. The Shimoni bar is taller, because 20 is more than 14.

That is a real chart, made from your own kind of data, in one line.
:::

## Make it fit to show someone

The bars are right, but a chart nobody can read is no use in a report. Three settings fix that. Each one
is just a word and a value:

- `main =` puts a **title** on top
- `ylab =` labels the **side**, so the reader knows the numbers are kilograms
- `col =` sets the **colour**

Press **Run**, then try changing the title, or the colour to `"darkgreen"`:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
barplot(
  totals$total_kg,
  names.arg = totals$gaul_2_name,
  main      = "Total catch by district",
  ylab      = "Kilograms",
  col       = "steelblue"
)
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** the same two bars, now blue, with a title above and "Kilograms" down the side.

This is the version you would paste into a report. Nothing about the numbers changed. You only made them
easier to read.
:::

## Now your own data

Time to draw your own records. A useful first question: **which gear brings in the most?**

It is the same two steps. Work out the totals, then draw them.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**One thing to know first.** A chart needs numbers to draw. If there is nothing to draw — because you are
**not signed in**, or your records came back empty — these last boxes show **red text** instead of a
picture.

The last line will read `need finite 'xlim' values`. It looks alarming, but it is only `barplot` saying
*"you gave me an empty table, so I cannot tell how wide to make the picture."* A few warnings about `min`
and `max` may appear above it. Ignore those and read the **last line**, as always.

Nothing is broken. Open this lesson from the **Data Academy** tab while signed in, and the charts will
appear.
:::

**Step one, the totals.** Press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
gear_totals <- landings |>
  group_by(gear) |>
  summarise(total_kg = sum(catch_kg, na.rm = TRUE))

gear_totals
```

**Step two, the picture.** Gear names are long, so this one adds `las = 2`, which turns the labels
sideways to make room for them. Press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
barplot(
  gear_totals$total_kg,
  names.arg = gear_totals$gear,
  main      = "Total catch by gear",
  ylab      = "Kilograms",
  col       = "steelblue",
  las       = 2
)
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** one bar for each fishing method in your records, with the tallest bar showing the
gear that brings in the most weight.

If the labels look cramped, that is normal on a small screen. Try removing `las = 2` and pressing **Run**
again to see the difference it makes.
:::

### Your turn: chart something else

Now you choose what to draw. The box below is the same two steps, with the **column blanked out**. Replace
both `______` with the **same column name**, then press **Run**.

Press **Hint** if you would like a suggestion.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_chart_column
#| envir: global
#| caption: "Chart your catch, grouped by a column you choose"
my_totals <- landings |>
  group_by(______) |>
  summarise(total_kg = sum(catch_kg, na.rm = TRUE))

barplot(
  my_totals$total_kg,
  names.arg = my_totals$______,
  main      = "My chart",
  ylab      = "Kilograms",
  col       = "steelblue",
  las       = 2
)
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_chart_column" }
Any column that holds **words** rather than numbers will work. Good ones to try:

- `gaul_2_name` — one bar for each district
- `catch_taxon` — one bar for each kind of fish

Put the **same** name in both blanks.
:::

::: { .hint exercise="ex_chart_column" }
If you choose `catch_taxon` you may get a great many bars, because there are many kinds of fish. That is
not a mistake. It is a sign that a chart with fewer groups, like `gaul_2_name`, is easier to read.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_chart_column" }
```r
my_totals <- landings |>
  group_by(gaul_2_name) |>
  summarise(total_kg = sum(catch_kg, na.rm = TRUE))

barplot(
  my_totals$total_kg,
  names.arg = my_totals$gaul_2_name,
  main      = "Total catch by district",
  ylab      = "Kilograms",
  col       = "steelblue",
  las       = 2
)
```
:::

## What you have learned

- A chart is a **table, drawn**. Always two steps: work out the totals, then draw them.
- **`barplot(heights, names.arg = labels)`** draws the bars.
- **`main =`**, **`ylab =`** and **`col =`** make it fit to show someone.
- **`las = 2`** turns the labels sideways when the names are long.

And one idea worth keeping: a chart never calculates anything. It only shows the numbers you already
worked out, so if a bar looks wrong, check the **totals** table above it.

## That is the whole course

You can now read your data, narrow it down, add it up, and draw it. That is enough to answer most of the
everyday questions your work asks of your records.

Keep the **recipe card** nearby. It has every command from the course on one page, so you do not have to
remember any of it.
